studies.title: The Thing That Falls Due
studies.meaning: A noun is stated, then queried, then queried again with a formula saying the listener has no way to know. The word itself comes from the root for something being true and for a debt falling due, so the day is named by the fact that everything provisional becomes actual. Only after three lines of naming does the surah supply content, and it does so through history rather than description: two peoples denied a day called the striking blow, and the first was destroyed by something named only as the overwhelming.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early, from the period when surahs were short, heavily rhymed and built around a single word held up for the listener. No occasion of revelation is reported. Thamud and Ad were not foreign examples to this audience; their ruins lay along the trade routes north and south of Mecca, and pre-Islamic poetry already used both peoples as bywords for a civilisation that had vanished.

keyTerms.note: From the root for truth and for a debt falling due. It names the day by the fact that everything provisional becomes actual then, so the word carries settlement rather than catastrophe.
A participle for a sound that knocks or a blow that strikes hard. The word is also the title of a later surah, where it receives the same three-line treatment this one gives its own opening word.
From a root for water breaking its banks. Commentators read it as the cry that destroyed Thamud, or as their own overreaching returning upon them, and the word occurs only here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debts in Mecca fell due at named seasons, and the language of a claim becoming enforceable was ordinary commercial speech. A man who owed could argue until the day arrived, and afterwards he could not. The word this surah opens with belongs to that world before it belongs to any other, which is why the audience heard a settlement date rather than only a disaster.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening three ayat use a formula the Quran deploys sparingly: the word, then a question about the word, then a second question saying the listener has no way to know it. Exactly the same three-step opening is given to another name for the same day at the head of a later surah, and that name is the one this passage uses in its fourth ayah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the day by truth rather than by destruction is the passage's real claim. What is coming is not primarily an event but a verification, in which what was arguable stops being arguable. The move into history then supplies a pattern rather than a proof: peoples who denied a day of striking were struck, which makes the argument inductive. The reader is handed ruins as evidence and left to draw the line forward.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the same three-step formula, using the word this passage introduces in its fourth line.
Tells the story of Thamud at length, including the warning they were given and refused.
Describes the wind sent against Ad, using the same rare adjective this surah gives it.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you have been telling yourself is probably fine, and find out whether it is. An unopened bill, a symptom, a message you have not replied to. This surah names the coming day by the fact that things stop being provisional. You can practise that on something small, and it takes an afternoon.

studies.title: Seven Nights, Eight Days
studies.meaning: The second people are handled in more detail than the first. The wind is given three descriptions, shrieking and cold and beyond restraint, and the duration is then specified with unusual precision: seven nights and eight days, qualified by a word the commentators read as consecutive, or as cutting off, or as leaving nothing behind. The result is one image. Bodies lying scattered like the hollow stumps of palm trees, which is what remains when a trunk has been emptied from inside.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Ad were remembered in Arabian tradition as a people of the southern sands, and their name survived in poetry and proverb long after the details had gone. The Quran assumes its audience knows who they were and supplies only the manner of their end. No occasion of revelation is reported. The passage belongs to a surah building its case from ruins the listeners could locate on a map.

keyTerms.note: A doubled form imitating a sound, used of a wind that howls. The lexicographers add coldness to the noise, so the word carries two sensations at once, and it appears three times in the Quran.
The commentators read it as successive without a gap, as severing, or as leaving nothing at all. The word occurs only here, and every reading agrees that the days ran without relief.
Used of a house whose roof has fallen in and of anything collapsed from within. Applied to palm stumps it makes the bodies look like something that gave way rather than something struck down.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A date palm was a household's long-term asset. It took years to bear, it survived drought that killed everything else, and a felled or hollowed trunk was the visible sign of a ruined holding. Storms of wind-driven sand were the region's most feared weather, able to strip a camp overnight. The simile joins the thing a settled family most dreaded losing to the force it most feared.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparison to fallen palm trunks appears twice in the Quran, here and in a passage of Al-Qamar describing the same people. Both places use the same three words for the image and then close it with different adjectives, one meaning torn up by the roots and one meaning hollow. It is the same picture taken from two positions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The precision about duration does particular work. A single instant of destruction can be read as an accident, and eight days cannot, so the passage insists on the count. It also leaves the wind entirely ordinary in kind; nothing unfamiliar is introduced, only something common that did not stop. That is the surah's method with every people it names, and it keeps the argument inside the world its audience already inhabited.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same simile of fallen palm trunks for the same people, with one word changed.
Names Ad's own confidence in their strength before describing the wind sent against them.
Shows them mistaking the approaching destruction for the rain cloud they had been hoping for.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you talk about a run of bad weather or bad luck lasting more than a day. Most of us shift, somewhere around the third day, from calling it chance to looking for a reason. This passage counts the days deliberately. Try noticing where your own threshold sits, the next time something goes on longer than expected.

studies.title: Carried On The Water
studies.meaning: The list continues and then turns. Pharaoh, those before him, and the overturned settlements are named together, charged with a single failing between them, and the seizure that followed is described with a word for something swollen past its size. Then the perspective changes without warning. Where every other people has been a they, the flood is put in the second person: when the water broke its banks, We carried you in the vessel that runs. The commentators note that every listener is being placed among the survivors.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The overturned settlements are the towns of Lot's people, named in the Quran by a word for being turned upside down, and their site lay on a trade route the Meccans used. Noah is not named here at all, only the vessel and the survivors. The commentators read the sudden second person as addressing the audience as descendants of those carried, which is how the surah ties them into the list.

keyTerms.note: A participle for being flipped over, applied to towns rather than to people. It appears twice in the Quran, both times inside a list of destroyed peoples, and it names the manner rather than the place.
From the root for growing and for a raised mound, the same root behind the word for increase on a debt. Applied to a seizure it means one beyond its expected size, and it occurs only here.
A participle meaning that which runs, used of a ship and of flowing water. Naming the ark this way describes it by its motion rather than by its construction or its size.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Meccans were not sailors, but they knew ships. Their caravans met Red Sea ports, and Abyssinian and Yemeni vessels were part of the trade they lived on; some of the early community would later cross that sea for refuge. A boat was a familiar object with an unfamiliar property, since it was the one thing that let a person survive an element which killed everything else.
studies.didYouKnow: The passage shifts from the third person to the second inside a single ayah. Every people before this is described as they, and then the flood is described as something that happened to you. The classical commentators treat such a change of address as a deliberate device, and here it places the reader inside the story at the one point where anybody survives.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Three peoples are given one charge between them, which compresses very different stories into a single failure: they disobeyed the messenger of their Lord. The passage then does something unusual with the flood by making it a rescue rather than a punishment, told from inside the boat. Judgement and preservation turn out to be one event described from two positions, and the reader is placed, without being asked, in the second.

crossReferences.why: Tells the flood from inside the ark at length, including who was carried and who was not.
Uses the same word for the overturned settlements, in another list of peoples who refused messengers.
Describes the same vessel and says it was left behind as a sign for anyone who would take one.

studies.applyIt: Trace one thing about your own life back four or five generations, to a point where somebody survived something. A migration, an illness, a war. Most families have one such point. This passage makes that move in a single line, and doing it yourself changes what a distant rescue is doing in your head.

studies.title: An Ear That Retains
studies.meaning: The purpose of the whole list is stated: it is to be a reminder, and to be retained by an ear that retains. The phrase is deliberately circular, and the commentators read the doubling as marking the difference between hearing a thing and keeping it. Then the surah moves to the day itself. One blast, the earth and the mountains lifted and crushed in a single crushing, and the sky splitting apart, described afterwards with a word for cloth worn so thin it gives way of itself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The surah has been reciting a list of destroyed peoples and now says what the list is for, which is the hinge of the whole chapter. No occasion of revelation is reported. The commentators note the repeated word single, one blast and one crushing, in a description that could easily have been extended, and they read the restraint as part of the effect.

keyTerms.note: A noun for the thing that brings something back to mind rather than for the memory itself. It marks the destroyed peoples as material for the listener rather than as a record kept for its own sake.
A participle from the root for a vessel that holds liquid without leaking. Applied to an ear it separates hearing from keeping, and the word occurs only here in the Quran.

Used of a rope fraying or a garment worn through, something that fails from weakness rather than from force. Applied to the sky it makes the split a collapse rather than a blow, and it appears only here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Waterskins were the technology a journey depended on. A skin that seeped was worse than useless, because the loss was discovered at the point where it could not be made good, and choosing and testing them was a real skill. The word used here for an ear that retains is the word for a container that holds without leaking, and the audience judged that quality before every departure.
studies.didYouKnow: Two words in this short passage occur nowhere else in the Quran: the one describing an ear that holds what it hears, and the one describing the sky as worn thin. This surah is unusually full of such words, and its rhyme is part of the reason, since through much of it nearly every line closes on the same syllable and the vocabulary bends to meet it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names its own purpose, which few passages do, and the purpose is cognitive rather than emotional. What is asked for is retention, and the doubled phrase concedes that most hearing is not that. It then makes the coming day sudden and singular, with one blast doing what could have been described as a process. Between the two halves lies the argument that what cannot be rehearsed has to be held in advance.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same blast and the condition of hearts on the day it arrives.
Names the same requirement, a heart present or an ear that genuinely attends.
Gives the same undoing of sky and earth as a sequence rather than as a single stroke.

studies.applyIt: Try keeping one sentence from something you read or hear today, without writing it down, until tomorrow morning. Most people cannot, and finding that out is the point of the exercise. This ayah distinguishes an ear that hears from an ear that holds, and there is no way to know which one you have except by testing it once.

studies.title: Eight Above Them
studies.meaning: The scene fills out. Angels stand along the edges of a sky that has just been described as giving way, and above them, on that day, eight carry the Throne of the Lord. The commentators are careful with the number, reporting it as given without explanation and declining to say what the eight are counting. Then the surah drops from the cosmic to the personal in one line. Everything about a person is displayed, no concealed thing stays concealed, and the first man to speak holds his record out and tells people to read it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This audience recognised angels as beings associated with God and disputed their nature rather than their existence, so the scene builds on shared ground. No occasion of revelation is attested. The commentators note that this is one of very few places in the Quran that puts a number on anything in that setting, and that the number is stated and then left entirely alone.

keyTerms.note: A plural for the sides or borders of a thing, used of the rim of a well and the margins of a valley. It occurs only here, placing the angels at the boundaries of a sky already described as failing.
The verb for goods laid out for inspection and for troops passed in review. It makes the exposure orderly and public rather than sudden, which is a particular kind of unpleasantness.
An interjection used when handing something over to a group. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it is the ordinary word a person uses across a table, which is what makes the line sound relieved.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A ruler's court in that world was arranged by proximity. Guards stood at the edges of the hall, officials nearer in, and the throne itself was carried in procession by named men whose position was both an honour and a job. Meccans who traded north had seen such arrangements in Byzantine and Persian territory. This scene uses that architecture exactly, then adds a public review of everybody present.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the very few places in the Quran that puts a number on anything in the unseen. The commentators transmit the eight without explaining it, and several say plainly that its meaning is not known. The same number happens to appear earlier in this surah, for the days of wind sent against Ad, with no connection drawn between the two.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing the exposure of every person immediately after the throne scene collapses an enormous distance into one line. The same day contains the edge of the sky and the contents of a private life, and the passage moves between them with no transition at all. The first speaker's reaction is then the surprise: he offers his record to be read by anyone, which makes vindication social rather than private.

crossReferences.why: Places angels around the Throne at the same moment, and gives what they are saying there.
Describes the same man given his record in the right hand and the ease that follows it.
Shows the reaction of those who find that nothing has been left out of the record.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you do that you would not want read out. Not a secret exactly, just something you keep in a slightly different account from the rest of your life. You do not need to confess it to anybody. This ayah says nothing hidden stays hidden, and naming the item to yourself is most of the work.

studies.title: Fruit Within Arm's Reach
studies.meaning: The reason for the man's confidence is given in his own words, and it is modest: he thought he would meet his account. The verb he uses is the one for supposing rather than for knowing, and the commentators discuss it, since an expectation held rather than a proof possessed is what carried him. What follows is described almost entirely by ease. A life he is content with, a garden set high, and clusters hanging low enough to take without reaching. Then an invitation to eat and drink, for what he sent on ahead.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has spent its first half on destroyed peoples and now sets out the alternative, briefly and without argument. No occasion of revelation is reported. The commentators note the structure: two men are described in matched ayat, each given a book and each given speech, though the second man's account is the longer of the two and both open with wording that is otherwise identical.

keyTerms.note: A verb covering everything from a guess to a settled conviction. Commentators read it here in its strong sense, but the word still names an expectation held rather than a fact possessed, which is the point.

An active participle attached to the life rather than to the man, so the grammar makes the living itself content. Arabic transfers a quality this way, and the effect is that nothing in it is straining.
From the root for nearness. Applied to fruit it names the detail that decides whether a garden is work or rest, since a harvest normally means climbing, and this word removes the climb.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Harvesting dates meant climbing. A man went up the trunk with a rope around himself and the tree, cut the clusters and lowered them, and falls were a known cause of injury in an oasis. The best fruit was usually the highest. A garden where the clusters hung at hand would have sounded, to that audience, like the labour being removed rather than the fruit being sweeter.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about clusters hanging within reach appears twice in the Quran, here and in a passage of Al-Insan, where the same word for the clusters is used and the shade is described as brought down low as well. Both places make their point through a detail of height rather than through any statement about abundance or quantity.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The man's own explanation is expectation, not achievement. He says he thought he would be held to account, and the passage lets that stand as the reason, which places the decisive thing inside a person's ordinary working assumptions rather than in any single act. The reward is then described by comfort rather than by honour, and the closing invitation attributes it to what he sent ahead, returning the credit to conduct.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same low-hanging clusters and adds shade brought down close over them.
Gives the same man his record in the right hand and an easy reckoning after it.
States the principle he is relying on, that whatever good is sent ahead is found with God.

studies.applyIt: Notice, once today, an assumption you are living by that you have never examined: that the work will be seen, that the effort counts somewhere. This man's whole account of himself is one such expectation, held quietly and shaping everything. Ask which of yours is doing that much work, and whether you would state it out loud.

studies.title: The Book In The Left Hand
studies.meaning: The matching line arrives, identical in construction to the earlier one and reversed at a single word. The same phrasing, the same handing over, the same first-person speech, except that the hand is the left and the sentence is a wish rather than an offer. What he wants is not a different record but no record at all. The commentators note that he does not dispute the contents anywhere in what follows; his objection is to the existence of the document itself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. Written records were the exception in Mecca rather than the rule, and the image of a personal ledger produced at a reckoning drew on the practice of the towns and empires around Arabia rather than on local custom. No occasion of revelation is reported for this ayah. It stands as the hinge between the two portraits the surah has been building.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for the left side, and also for the north. Right and left work here as a notation for the outcome rather than as a description of anything a person did with either hand.

A particle of wishing for what cannot be had, used in the Quran for regret arriving after the possibility has closed. It introduces speech that changes nothing, which is why it recurs in scenes like this.
The final letter is written only to mark a pause in recitation and is dropped when the reading runs on. Six words in this surah carry it, all of them inside the speech of these two men.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Deeds in Mecca were remembered, not filed. A man's reputation was carried by the people who had dealt with him, and a dispute was settled by testimony and by oath. The idea of a written personal record would have sounded foreign and faintly menacing, since a document does not soften with time and cannot be talked round the way a witness can.
studies.didYouKnow: The two men's opening lines are word for word identical except for the hand named. Arabic makes the parallel exact, so a listener hears the second as the first one failing. After that the two diverge sharply: the first man's speech ends within two ayat, while the second man's runs on through five before it is cut off.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The wish is precise and it is telling. He does not ask for the record to be wrong; he asks for it not to exist. That concedes the accuracy of the account while rejecting the fact of accountability itself, which the commentators treat as the objection underneath every other one. The passage also gives him speech at length, which is a form of respect: the losing case is put in the first person and allowed to state itself.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same man given his record from behind his back, and what he calls out afterwards.
Puts the record in a person's hand and tells them to read it as their own reckoner.
Records a comparable wish, that the person had been dust rather than face the account.

studies.applyIt: Think of a running record you keep and do not enjoy: a bank statement, a fitness app, a shared calendar of everything you have agreed to. Open one of them today. The instinct in this ayah is the wish that the record did not exist, and the small version of it is available every time you decline to look.

studies.title: My Wealth Did Nothing
studies.meaning: The speech continues and narrows. He says he never knew what his account was, wishes the death he died had finished the matter, and then names two things by their loss: his money did not avail him, and his authority has perished. The commentators note that both nouns take the same pausal ending, so the two losses rhyme against each other. Then the speech is cut off mid-scene by an order given about him rather than to him, and the register shifts from lament to command.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience included men whose standing rested on exactly the two things named here, inherited wealth and a position in the tribal order, and several early surahs address them by those assets. No occasion of revelation is attested for these ayat. The commentators observe that the man is never identified, which leaves the speech available to anyone in the audience who recognised the inventory.

keyTerms.note: A participle from the root for concluding a matter and for passing a final judgement. He uses it of the death he has already died, wishing it had settled everything, and the word occurs only here.

The plain word for property, given the pausal ending that runs through this passage. It appears in this form only here, and the possessive carries the weight, since the complaint is about something owned.
A noun for authority backed either by force or by argument. Commentators read it as his standing among people, or as any case he might have made, and it appears in this form only here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Two things made a Meccan secure: what he owned and who would stand with him. Wealth bought protection and protection preserved wealth, and the two were not really separable. A man stripped of both was in genuine danger, since the town had no institution that would defend a person with neither. The pair named in this speech is the exact inventory of a Meccan's safety.
studies.didYouKnow: Four words in this man's speech, and two in the other man's, end with a letter written only to mark a pause and dropped when the recitation runs on. All six fall within eleven ayat of this surah, which gives the two speeches a sound entirely their own, and that sound stops the moment the order to seize him begins.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The complaint is not that the two things were wrong to have, but that they turned out not to apply. Nothing is said against wealth in itself here; what is denied is its jurisdiction. Read alongside the order that follows, the passage makes a quiet point about categories, since the man is still speaking the language of a world where his assets counted, and the sentence passed on him does not answer him in that language at all.

crossReferences.why: States the same failure in a few words, that a man's wealth and his gains did not avail him.
Names the day on which neither wealth nor sons will be of any use to anybody.
Describes arriving alone, with everything a person relied on left behind them.

studies.applyIt: Pick one possession you would find genuinely hard to lose and imagine, for thirty seconds, that it is already gone. Not as a fear exercise. Just to find out what else moves when you take it away. This man learns the answer at the point where nothing can be adjusted, and half a minute now is a much cheaper way to find out.

studies.title: He Did Not Urge It
studies.meaning: The sentence is issued in short imperatives, and then the reasons follow. Two are given. He did not believe in God the Great, and he did not urge the feeding of the destitute. The commentators handle the second carefully: the charge is not that he fed nobody but that he did not press anyone else to, which makes it a failure of advocacy rather than of almsgiving. A single line then closes the passage by saying he has no close friend there, which answers the protection he had relied on.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The pairing of belief with feeding the poor runs through the earliest surahs and appears in almost identical wording in more than one of them, which the commentators read as the two headings under which the early message was summarised. No occasion of revelation is attested for these ayat. Mecca had visible destitution alongside considerable wealth, and the surahs of this period return to it repeatedly.

keyTerms.note: A verb for inciting somebody else to act rather than for acting yourself. Naming this instead of the giving makes the failure social: he never made the case for feeding people to anyone around him.
From a root for being stilled or brought to a standstill. It names poverty by its effect, a person whose circumstances have stopped them moving, rather than by a measure of what they lack.

The word for someone bound closely enough to intervene on your behalf, used of kin and of sworn friends. In the tribal order such a person was the whole of a man's protection, and the ayah says there is none.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Feeding the poor in Mecca was a matter of household decision, not of any collected fund. A man of standing could set the tone for his clan simply by what he said at a gathering, and a word from him either opened other men's hands or closed them. That is why the charge lands on urging rather than on giving: in that society an influential man's silence had a measurable cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The same two failures, refusing belief and not pressing others to feed the poor, are paired in another short surah of this period, where they appear in the same order and in nearly the same words. The recurrence is striking, since among all the charges available the Quran twice selects exactly these two and sets them side by side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two charges are listed and neither is a crime against a specific person. One is a refusal of belief and the other is a failure to advocate, which together define wrongdoing more broadly than any inventory of acts would. The Quran also pairs them without argument, as though the connection were self-evident. The final line then removes the one thing that had made all of it survivable, which is other people.

crossReferences.why: Pairs the same two failures in the same order, denial of the reckoning and not urging food.
Puts the same charge in the second person, about honouring orphans and pressing for the poor.
Describes the opposite, those in whose wealth a known right belongs to the one who asks.

studies.applyIt: Say something out loud this week in favour of a person or a cause that nobody in the room is speaking for. Not a donation. A sentence. The charge in this passage is not against a man who gave nothing; it is against a man who never made the case to anybody, and that is correctable in one conversation.

studies.title: Sworn By The Unseen
studies.meaning: The description of punishment ends with food named by a single obscure word, glossed as what runs from a wound when it is washed, and reserved for those who err. Then the surah turns without transition to an oath, and the oath is unusual: it swears by what the listeners can see and by what they cannot, which between them leave nothing out. What it establishes is the origin of the speech being heard. This is the word of a noble messenger, and the commentators differ over whether the messenger meant is the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) or the angel who brought it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The two accusations the following ayat answer, poet and soothsayer, were the categories available to this audience for a man producing extraordinary speech, and both were respectable rather than insulting in themselves. No occasion of revelation is reported. The oath form here is characteristic of the earliest surahs, where an assertion about revelation is regularly preceded by a sworn preface.

keyTerms.note: From the root for washing. Commentators gloss it as what runs from a wound when it is cleaned, and the word occurs only here, so the tradition has no second passage from which to define it.

The verb for seeing with attention rather than for merely having eyes open. Swearing by what is seen and what is not covers everything that exists, using the audience's own faculty as the dividing line.
The adjective covers generosity, high birth and worth together. The identical phrase appears in one other surah, where the description that follows it makes an angel the more likely reference.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had categories for remarkable speech, and both are named in the lines that follow this oath. A poet spoke for a tribe and could raise or ruin a reputation. A soothsayer produced rhymed oracular phrases and was consulted about disputes and lost property. Both were paid, both were recognised professions, and an audience hearing something extraordinary reached for one of the two labels automatically.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase calling this the word of a noble messenger occurs twice in the Quran, here and in a passage of At-Takwir. In this surah it is followed by a denial that the speaker is a poet or a soothsayer, while there it is followed by a description of strength and standing before the Lord of the Throne. The same phrase points in two directions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The oath sworn on the unseen alongside the seen makes a claim before the sentence it introduces does. It puts the invisible in the same inventory as the visible and swears by both in one breath. What follows then attributes the speech to a messenger rather than to its hearer, which the commentators read either as prophecy or as transmission by an angel. On either reading the point is that the speaker is not the source.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase and then describes the messenger in terms that suit an angel.
States the same point about the source, that what is spoken is revelation taught to him.
Swears an oath of the same kind before making a comparable claim about this recitation.

studies.applyIt: Notice this week how fast you assign a category to something unfamiliar. A person's manner, a claim, a piece of news. The label arrives before the assessment does, and it usually ends the assessment. This passage answers two labels its audience reached for automatically, and the useful exercise is catching your own in the second before it lands.

studies.title: Had He Made It Up
studies.meaning: Two denials, each followed by a short comment on the audience rather than on the claim: little do you believe, little do you take heed. Then the positive statement, that this is sent down from the Lord of the Worlds. What follows is the surah's most striking move. A hypothetical is entertained in which the messenger had attributed sayings to God falsely, and the consequence is described physically, as a seizure by the right hand. The commentators note that the punishment imagined falls on him and not on his audience.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. A poet and a soothsayer were the two available explanations for what the Meccans were hearing, and both are denied by name across the earliest surahs. No occasion of revelation is attested for these ayat. The hypothetical about false attribution is read by the commentators as answering a suspicion the audience genuinely held, that the message was being shaped to suit the man carrying it.

keyTerms.note: A recognised profession in Arabia, consulted about disputes and lost property, whose pronouncements came in short rhymed phrases. The word appears twice in the Quran, both times denied of the messenger.

A verbal noun naming the process rather than the product, and formed to suggest something delivered in stages. It answers the two labels by placing the origin above the speaker rather than by praising him.
A form of the verb to say meaning to invent speech and put it in another's mouth. Arabic marks the fabrication inside the verb pattern, so no separate word for falsehood is needed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rhymed prose was the soothsayer's medium, and the audience knew its rhythms well enough to test a claim against them. Poetry was memorised, judged in public and attributed with care, since a line placed in the wrong poet's mouth was a matter of honour. Attribution mattered in that culture in a way that carried real weight, and the hypothetical here is framed in exactly those terms.
studies.didYouKnow: The two professions denied here, poet and soothsayer, were the respectable explanations available in Arabia for extraordinary speech, and the Quran denies both of them in several early surahs. Neither denial is an insult to those trades. What is rejected is the category itself, since both were understood as human crafts with techniques that could be learned.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The hypothetical is a strange thing for a scripture to contain. It imagines its own bearer inventing content and states what would follow, which stakes the message's credibility on his continued restraint rather than on his rank. The commentators note that the imagined seizure is described without mercy and without appeal. Read plainly, the passage sets a heavier penalty on false attribution than on any of the charges the surah has been answering.

crossReferences.why: Denies the same two labels and then asks whether they claim he invented the message himself.
Has the messenger say he cannot alter the revelation of his own accord in any way.
States that poetry was neither taught to him nor suitable for what he has been given.

studies.applyIt: Check one thing you have repeated as fact this month and find out where you got it. Not to catch yourself out. Just to see how many steps back the chain goes before it stops somewhere. This passage treats putting words in another's mouth as the gravest thing in its argument, and most of us pass on attributions we have never traced.

studies.title: Nobody Could Have Stopped It
studies.meaning: The hypothetical completes itself with an anatomical detail, the severing of the vessel that carries life, and then a flat statement that not one of the listeners could have held the consequence off him. After that the surah turns to what the message is for those who receive it. It is a reminder to those who guard themselves, and the next line concedes something rarely stated: among the listeners there are people who will call it false. The last line calls the message itself a grief for those who reject it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early, addressed to a mixed audience in which acceptance and rejection were both visible daily. No occasion of revelation is reported. The commentators note the concession in the middle of these ayat, where the Quran says plainly that some of its hearers will refuse it, and read it as a statement about the composition of the audience rather than about anybody's final outcome.

keyTerms.note: The great vessel carrying blood from the heart, named specifically rather than by any general word for a vein. It occurs only here, and the precision is what makes the hypothetical concrete.
A plural participle for those who stand between two things and keep them apart, from the same root as the barrier set between two seas. This plural form appears only here in the Quran.
A noun for the ache of realising too late what had been available. Calling the message itself this, rather than the outcome, makes the source of the grief the thing that was offered and refused.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Slaughtering animals was ordinary domestic knowledge, and everyone knew which vessels ended a life quickly. Anatomy was practical rather than theoretical, and a herder could name what he cut and why. The word used here is precise in that practical sense, so the audience registered a specific thing rather than a general image for killing, which is what gives the line its edge.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the artery in this passage occurs only once in the Quran, and the plural word for those who could have prevented the seizure occurs only once as well. Both are technical: one anatomical, one taken from the vocabulary of physical barriers, and the same root behind the second is used elsewhere of the divider set between two bodies of water.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things sit oddly together here and belong together. The first is the claim that the bearer of this message would have been stopped at once had he tampered with it. The second is an admission that some who hear it will refuse it. Taken together they separate the message's reliability from its reception, arguing that being widely refused is not evidence against something, and saying so about itself.

crossReferences.why: Names the same message as healing and guidance for the people who actually receive it.
Says the same revelation is healing for some and only loss for those who wrong themselves.
Uses the same root for a barrier, set there between two bodies of water rather than between people.

studies.applyIt: Think of one true thing you have been given and have not used: advice, a skill, a warning, a book somebody pressed on you. The last line of this passage calls the message a grief for those who refuse it, which locates the pain in what was offered rather than in any penalty. Pick one and take it up this week.

studies.title: The Truth Of Certainty
studies.meaning: Two lines close the surah. The first names what has been described using a phrase built from two words for certainty, one governing the other, which Arabic uses to mark the highest of several degrees. The commentators set it beside two related phrases from elsewhere, one for certainty known and one for certainty seen, and read this one as certainty arrived at. Then the last line turns from argument to instruction, and the instruction is not to believe or to act but to glorify the name of the Lord.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The surah has moved through destroyed peoples, the day itself, two men and their records, and a defence of where the revelation comes from, and it closes by handing the listener something to do rather than something more to consider. No occasion of revelation is attested. The identical closing line appears twice in another surah of the same period.

keyTerms.note: Two words for the sure and the certain placed in a possessive construction, which Arabic uses for emphasis of the strongest kind. The commentators rank the phrase above two related ones used elsewhere.
An imperative meaning to declare God far from any deficiency. It closes an argument with a practice rather than with a conclusion, and the verb implies removing something rather than adding praise.
An adjective of sheer magnitude, used in the Quran of the Throne, of the Day, and of a great attainment. Attached here to the Lord, it closes a surah that has been describing scale throughout.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan speech ended arguments with a proverb or a line of verse the audience could carry away and repeat. Poetry did this constantly, closing a long recitation with something portable. The last ayah here works the same way and is short enough to say under the breath while walking, which is how a formula survives in a culture that remembers rather than writes.
studies.didYouKnow: This final ayah appears three times in the Quran, word for word: twice in Al-Waqi'ah and once at the end of this surah. The line before it appears twice, in those same two places. Al-Waqi'ah closes on exactly this pair of sentences, so two chapters of the same period end with an identical two-line ending.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending on an imperative rather than on a conclusion changes what the surah has been doing. Everything before it is argument and description, and the last line asks for a practice instead of assent. What it asks for is also negative in form: not praise added but deficiency denied, which suits a chapter that has spent its length insisting things are not what its audience assumed. The response to certainty here is a habit, not a verdict.

crossReferences.why: Closes another surah with the identical two lines, in the same order and the same wording.
Uses two related phrases for degrees of certainty, both ranked below the one used here.
Opens a surah with the same imperative to glorify the name of the Lord.

studies.applyIt: Say the last line of this surah once, out loud, when you finish reading it. Not as a ritual to add to your day. As the thing the surah itself asks for at the end of its argument, in place of a summary. Notice that it takes three seconds, and that the chapter chose it over a conclusion.
